title: The Fall of Proud Babylon
overview: Isaiah announces that the LORD will bring distant armies against Babylon, the empire that would later conquer Judah, and leave its proud capital an empty ruin.

parts.label: An army is summoned (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: A flag raised on a bare hilltop was a signal for troops to gather, and here the LORD is pictured as the general calling up armies from faraway lands against Babylon. The soldiers are called his weapons, though they fight for their own reasons and do not know him.

parts.label: Panic on the day (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: The "day of the LORD" means a time when God steps in to judge, and here it falls on Babylon. Its people lose all strength and courage, writhing like a woman in labor and staring at each other with burning faces.

parts.label: Sky darkens, earth shakes (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: The target widens to the pride of tyrants everywhere, survivors become as rare as the finest gold, and the sun, moon and stars go dark. Many read the dark sky as a picture of a world order collapsing; others also expect it literally at the end of history, and Christians hear it echoed in Jesus' words about the end of the age.

parts.label: Flight and slaughter (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: Foreigners living in Babylon scatter home like hunted gazelles, and anyone caught is killed. The poem does not soften the atrocities ancient conquering armies committed: children killed, homes looted, women raped.

parts.label: The Medes named (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: The attackers are the Medes, a people from what is now northwestern Iran, who cannot be bribed with silver or gold to spare a life. Their archers show no mercy to young men or to children.

parts.label: A home for jackals (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: Babylon, the jewel of its world, will be wiped out as completely as Sodom and Gomorrah, the cities destroyed in Genesis, until only wild animals live in its palaces. In history, Babylon fell to the Persian king Cyrus and his Median allies in 539 BC with little fighting, and it emptied slowly into ruins over the following centuries.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this chapter speaks only of ancient Babylon's fall or also points ahead to a final judgment on the whole world at the end of history.
think: When a powerful empire that crushed others is itself brought down, does that feel to you more like justice, more like further suffering, or both at once?
